Let each square have side length \(2\), with coordinates
\[
B=(0,0),\quad R=(2,0),\quad T=(0,2).
\]

### Square I
The top midpoint is \((1,2)\). The two lines have equations
\[
y=2-x \qquad\text{and}\qquad y=2x.
\]
Thus their intersection is
\[
2x=2-x\implies x=\frac23,\quad y=\frac43.
\]
The shaded triangle has base \(2\) (the left side) and altitude \(\frac23\), so
\[
S_I=\frac12(2)\left(\frac23\right)=\frac23.
\]

### Square II
The right midpoint is \((2,1)\). The lines are
\[
y=2-x \qquad\text{and}\qquad y=\frac{x}{2}.
\]
Their intersection satisfies
\[
\frac{x}{2}=2-x\implies x=\frac43,\quad y=\frac23.
\]
The shaded triangle has base \(1\) (half the right side) and horizontal altitude
\[
2-\frac43=\frac23.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_{II}=\frac12(1)\left(\frac23\right)=\frac13.
\]

### Square III
The bottom and right midpoints are \((1,0)\) and \((2,1)\). The lines are
\[
y=2-2x \qquad\text{and}\qquad y=\frac{x}{2}.
\]
Hence
\[
2-2x=\frac{x}{2}\implies x=\frac45,\quad y=\frac25.
\]
The shaded triangle has base \(2\) and altitude \(\frac45\), giving
\[
S_{III}=\frac12(2)\left(\frac45\right)=\frac45.
\]

Thus
\[
\frac13<\frac23<\frac45,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\text{E: }S_{II}<S_I<S_{III}}.
\]
